#4283. Volkswagen’s new ID. Buzz Beach electric camper goes on sale, starting at over $70,000

Volkswagen opened orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK, an electric van built for camping and overnight stays, with a fold-out mattress and more. It’s not exactly cheap, though, starting at over $70,000.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

Volkswagen opened orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK this week, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it starts at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is offering a few financing deals to get you started, with prices from £555 ($726) a month, including a £6,500 ($8,500) deposit.

What about those in the US? Will Volkswagen bring the electric camper to the States?

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a new Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

#4282. Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging

Blood vessels naturally become less flexible with age, and certain diseases can accelerate this process. As blood vessels stiffen, the risk of cardiovascular disease and premature death increases.

One factor that can contribute to this damage is an excess of phosphate in the bloodstream. Although elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is relatively uncommon in the general population, it occurs much more frequently in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), whose kidneys gradually lose their ability to filter waste from the blood.

Scientists at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have identified a kidney protein that plays a critical role in regulating blood phosphate levels. The discovery could have particularly important implications for people living with CKD.

In a new study published in October 2026, the researchers found that a deficiency of this protein caused blood vessels to stiffen more rapidly and shortened lifespan in animal models. These effects were especially pronounced when the animals consumed a diet high in phosphate. Reducing phosphate intake helped alleviate some of the damage.

The findings point to a potential new target for medications and other therapies designed to maintain healthy phosphate levels. Such treatments could eventually help people with CKD improve their overall health and potentially live longer.

"Phosphate is really underestimated in terms of longevity in all mammals. The higher the concentration of phosphate in the blood, the shorter the lifespan," says Makoto Miyazaki, PhD, a research professor in the Division of Renal Diseases and Hypertension and the senior author of the new study.

How Excess Phosphate Accelerates Blood Vessel Aging

Phosphorus is an essential nutrient that helps build and maintain strong bones. It occurs naturally in a wide variety of whole foods, including meat, poultry, fish, whole grains, nuts, legumes, and dairy products, generally in the form of organic phosphate compounds. Food manufacturers also add phosphates to processed foods and beverages to improve flavor and extend shelf life.

Although phosphorus is necessary for good health, excessive levels in the blood (hyperphosphatemia) can trigger a series of damaging biological changes. Phosphate additives may be particularly concerning because the body absorbs them more rapidly and efficiently than the organic phosphates naturally present in whole foods.

Persistently elevated phosphate levels can cause smooth muscle cells within blood vessel walls to behave more like cells responsible for building bone. As a result, these cells begin depositing calcium phosphate crystals resembling those found in bones, causing the blood vessels to harden (or calcify).

Healthy blood vessels are flexible, allowing them to expand and contract in response to changing blood flow demands. Calcification compromises this flexibility, effectively accelerating vascular aging and potentially contributing to numerous age-related health problems throughout the body.

A Hidden Protein Helps Maintain Phosphate Balance

Under normal circumstances, the kidneys remove excess phosphate from the bloodstream before it reaches harmful levels. As CKD progresses, however, declining kidney function makes it increasingly difficult for the body to eliminate phosphate and other substances.

Maintaining the right amount of phosphate requires continuous adjustments. After the kidneys filter phosphate from the blood, a portion is eliminated through urine, while the remainder is returned to the circulation. A protein known as NPT2A is responsible for reabsorbing approximately 75% of the filtered phosphate, preventing the body from losing too much phosphorus.

When phosphate levels are already elevated, however, this recycling mechanism can become problematic. Miyazaki and his colleagues discovered that another protein, called TMEM174, acts as a natural brake on this process. By binding to NPT2A, it limits the amount of phosphate being reabsorbed into the bloodstream.

Protein Deficiency Shortens Lifespan in Animal Models

The latest findings highlight the importance of TMEM174 in maintaining healthy phosphate levels. Animals deficient in the protein struggled to regulate phosphate in their blood, experienced increased vascular calcification, and had significantly shorter lifespans.

"We don't fully understand how yet, but somehow TMEM174 is destabilizing NPT2A," says Miyazaki. "And without enough TMEM174, homeostasis is disrupted."

A deficiency of TMEM174 appears to result primarily from genetic factors rather than chronic kidney disease itself. However, the research suggests that people with CKD who also have insufficient levels of this protein could be particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of excess phosphate.

A Potential New Target for Protecting Blood Vessels

Miyazaki hopes the discovery will lead to treatments that reduce the amount of excess phosphate the kidneys return to the bloodstream.

Dietary changes may provide some benefit, particularly by reducing consumption of fast food, deli meats, sodas, and other processed products that contain large amounts of phosphate. However, Miyazaki explains that managing phosphate levels through diet alone can be challenging, especially for people with CKD. Because phosphate is present in such a wide range of foods, avoiding it is virtually impossible.

In future research, Miyazaki plans to investigate these kidney proteins further, along with the hormones involved in maintaining the body's chemical balance. He also wants to better understand why calcium accumulation in blood vessels is so common among people with CKD.

For now, identifying the role of TMEM174 represents an important advance in understanding how the body regulates phosphate. It could also help lay the groundwork for new approaches to improving the health of people whose phosphate balance is disrupted.

"Scientists have been studying phosphate homeostasis for over 100 years, so to still find a new protein that regulates phosphate is kind of unique," says Miyazaki.

Materials provided by University of Colorado School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4281. Volvo A40 Electric articulated haul trucks get to work in the UK

After becoming the world’s first all-electric 40 ton class articulated haul truck into regular series production earlier this year, the Volvo A40 has finally reached its first customers in the UK – and they wasted no time putting the big BEV to work on one of the nation’s largest, most important infrastructure projects.

More than sixty years after Volvo’s “Gravel Charlie” invented the articulated hauler, Volvo CE has delivered four customer A40 Electric articulated haul trucks to BMJV (a joint venture between Bouygues Travaux Publics and J Murphy & Sons) for use on the Lower Thames Crossing, further demonstrating that zero-emission machines are ready to move material at scale at major job sites right now.

“Going electric today is no longer about compromise, it’s about the benefits,” explains Shaun Pidcock, Lower Thames Crossing Programme Director at BMJV. “These remarkable machines show that even the heaviest jobs can be done cleanly, and in a way that is better for those working on or living near our sites.”

The Lower Thames Crossing project is approximately 14.3 miles long, and includes more than 2.5 miles of tunnels criss-crossing beneath the River Thames. Once finished, the project will connect the Kent and Essex meters, and promises to nearly double road capacity across the east side of London while becoming the first major infrastructure program in Britain completed with carbon-neutral construction.

By using the next generation of construction machinery to make the Lower Thames Crossing Britain’s greenest road today, we are helping the industry set a new standard for tomorrow and make diesel-powered sites a thing of the past.

Since grid power isn’t available on site, BMJV is using fuel cell generators fueled by British-manufactured green hydrogen to charge the A40s. The generators produce no exhaust emissions and are noticeably quieter than combustion machines, further improving living and working conditions for the humans around the site.

The “40” in the A40 Electric’s badge refers to the truck’s whopping 40 ton (39 tonne) payload capacity. Once loaded up, the hauler’s 350 kW (about 470 hp) electric motor sends power through a torque-amplifying gear reduction gearbox that, depending on how you do the math, delivers some 200,000 lb-ft of “at the wheel” torque. More than enough twisting force, in other words, to match the performance of diesel and possibly enough to have a measurable impact on the rotational speed of a planet.

That motor draws power from a 540 kWh li-ion battery good for up to six hours of continuous operation, but the hauler’s advanced regenerative braking system usually collects enough energy during operation to make it good for a full day’s shift. And, if there’s a Circle K nearby, operators can plug their A40 Electric into a 350 kW DC fast charger and get their battery from 10% to 90% in about an hour.

#4280. Dually Noted: The Reasons Why Some Pickup Trucks and Vans Come with Dual Rear Wheels

Dually pickup trucks and vans may look tough, but these models have four rear wheels and tires for reasons that have nothing to do with vanity.

The term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers. Namely, one: Don’t all vehicles have two rear wheels? Good work, detective. The dual part, however, refers to the number of rear wheels on each side. Confusing? Sure. But consider yourself a member of an elite club. Send away for your decoder ring now.

You’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans. Out in the real world, you’re likely to observe dually pickups towing big, heavy trailers, often using a gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch.

DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling. Simply put, DRW vehicles are meant to handle big loads.

Automakers go the DRW route on configurations of their heavy-duty trucks and vans designed for hauling and/or towing heavy loads. Having those extra tires means more contact patch over which to distribute the weight. It’s the same basic principle that’s used on semi trucks—having 18 or so wheels spread across the semi tractor and its trailer allows the rig to carry literal tons.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

On dually trucks, the wider stance helps increase stability as well. You can think of the two extra wheels like outriggers, keeping the truck better planted in the face of crosswinds or in turns.

The main drawbacks of a dually setup are somewhat obvious. You have to worry about six tires instead of four, which in turn makes tire replacement more expensive. For dually trucks, the extra wheels sit outside the normal pickup-bed envelope, necessitating flared fenders to cover the extra rubber.

Maneuvering a big SRW truck or van is difficult enough. Predictably, the additional width of a DRW vehicle only adds to the challenge. It’s why many dually trucks end up with a blemish or two on at least one rear fender. The fenders of newer dually pickups are made from lighter-weight fiberglass instead of steel, so they’re less likely to bend and more prone to cracking when they meet a stationary object.

This isn’t the case with most dually full-size vans. So-equipped vans add their additional tires inboard, which eliminates the need for flared rear fenders. The consequence of this arrangement is a slight reduction in outright cargo space due to the wheel wells extending further into the cabin.

Ever wonder why the front wheels of a dually truck or van have a severe outward dish to them? It’s so that all the wheels match and are therefore interchangeable should you need to use the spare. This dished design allows the rear wheels on one side to mate up with each other, which enables the use of two rear tires on both sides of the vehicle.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

The need for a dually comes down to capability. DRWs may be necessary to comfortably pull a fully laden horse trailer, a giant camper, various types of farm equipment, or the crops they help sow and reap. To get an idea of how much more a dually can handle, an SRW heavy-duty truck may be rated for a little more than 20,000 pounds of trailer weight on a bumper-mounted hitch, while the DRW variant of the same basic truck with a gooseneck hitch can pull almost twice the weight.

The difference isn’t as great with dual-rear-wheel versus SRW vans, mostly because both use bumper-mounted hitches. A DRW van may be able to tow as much as 50 percent more weight than a comparable SRW version. With some vans, towing capacity actually goes down when you add two rear wheels. Why go the dually route, then? Because that extra rubber is advantageous to rear-end stability—particularly when a van’s loaded up at, or near, its maximum payload capacity.

Dually setups are available on heavy-duty versions of full-size pickups and some large vans. Those looking for a pickup truck with a bed can choose this setup on the Chevrolet Silverado HD, GMC Sierra HD, Ram HD, and Ford F-series Super Duty.

In the realm of enclosed passenger and cargo vans, only the Ford Transit and Mercedes-Benz Sprinter offer available DRW configurations. You’ll also often find DRWs in use on cutaway and chassis-cab versions of these trucks and vans, which are used in the aftermarket to build things such as box trucks, tow trucks, and RVs.

In some international markets, where full-size pickups are much less common, automakers produce DRW versions of their sub-full-size pickups.

As with any towing or hauling exercise, make sure you understand the limits of your specific vehicle before loading it up or hitching a trailer to the back. Consider what you’re likely to tow or haul when shopping for your workhorse, and follow the manufacturer’s guidance on loading so you stay safe and avoid putting too much strain on the vehicle.

Dually is a term used for a pickup truck or van with dual rear wheels (DRW).

A dually pickup truck or van has two wheels and tires on each side of its rear axle for a grand total of four rear wheels and tires.

You do not need a CDL to drive a full-size pickup truck or an enclosed cargo or passenger van with dual rear wheels (DRWs).

Pedants will note that even a rear-wheel-drive dually relies on its engine to power four wheels (the four back ones). In a technical sense, however, a rear-drive dually is a two-wheel-drive vehicle, since power is sent to the drive wheels via two axle shafts. Similarly, though a four-wheel-drive-equipped dually may power a total of six wheels, the engine’s power only reaches the drive wheels via a total of four axle shafts (two at each end).

#4279. It’s official: Battlefield 6 is 2025's best-selling game, but Black Ops 7 still managed to be November’s top-seller

2025 will be remembered for many things, but in the ultra-competitive games industry, it’s going to be thought of as the year Battlefield 6 did what many thought couldn’t happen.

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including new entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

However, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

Spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a big impact.

#4278. Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.

Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly.

After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022.

"This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.

Reducing the Risks of Common Prescription Drugs

Older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination.

"A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so important for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety."

To identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders over the period from 2011 to 2022. They compared individuals prescribed at least one potentially inappropriate medication with those who had not received any of these drugs.

Medication Safety Has Improved, but Risks Remain

Although the study did not examine what caused the decline in exposure to potentially harmful medications, Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians over the past two decades. The gradual but sustained improvement may reflect broader advances in geriatric medicine and efforts to make prescription drug use safer.

"We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period," he says. "However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good."

Older adults, even those without cognitive disorders, are particularly susceptible to harmful drug interactions and inappropriate prescriptions. In some cases, these complications can increase the risk of death. These dangers are a central focus of Team Alice, an ongoing interdisciplinary research initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety.

Team Alice takes its name from Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 following a prescription for a muscle relaxant identified as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognized within the health care system, and Brennan died following six weeks of preventable complications.

Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared her mother's experience with University at Buffalo researchers in the hope of bringing about systemic changes that would spare other patients and families from similar harm.

Hsu began the new study shortly after joining the university's pharmacy school and Team Alice, where he works in the UB Patient Safety Learning Laboratory.

"This work extends a series of national analyses our group has published on potentially inappropriate medications, quality of life, and health care use in older adults," says David Jacobs, PharmD, PhD, associate professor of pharmacy practice and a principal investigator on Team Alice.

"It is especially important as older adults with cognitive disorders are the least able to tolerate medications that worsen memory or thinking, yet nearly one in three are still receiving them. Most of these patients have a regular source of care so these medications can be identified and addressed with their care team."

Improving Medication Safety for Older Adults

Other contributors to the study included Team Alice's fellow principal investigators Ranjit Singh, MD, associate professor and interim chair of the Department of Family Medicine at UB's Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, and Robert Wahler, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice.

Collin Clark, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice, and Steven Feuerstein, an information systems analyst at the Jacobs School, also contributed to the research.

The findings underscore the value of thorough medication reviews during routine outpatient appointments. The researchers also suggest incorporating clinical assessment tools such as the Drug Burden Index into acute and outpatient care. Such tools can help health care professionals assess the combined effects of medications that act on the central nervous system and potentially prevent avoidable complications.

Further research is needed to establish whether improving medication use can enhance quality of life and reduce hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older adults experiencing cognitive difficulties.

A Rapidly Aging Population Raises New Concerns

The findings arrive at a significant moment in global demographic history. According to a recent report from the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older now outnumber children from birth through age 5 worldwide for the first time in human history.

However, greater longevity does not necessarily translate into more years of good health. The same report indicates that nearly 75% of adults age 65 and older have at least two chronic health conditions. Managing multiple illnesses often requires taking more medications, some of which may have detrimental effects on the aging body and brain.

"This is an issue that has been building for decades, but the growth of the older adult population has arrived sooner than we expected," Hsu says. "This means that health care professionals need to pay closer attention than ever to medication safety, especially for older adults experiencing cognitive decline or other complex health concerns."

Materials provided by University at Buffalo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4275. Ford’s Next Le Mans Dream Is Finally Here: Meet the GT41

FoMoCo’s latest race car was built with one goal in mind: Get back on the top step of the Le Mans podium.

You’re probably aware that all the way back in 1963, Ford tried (unsuccessfully) to buy Ferrari from old Enzo. “Il Commendatore” quite famously used the offer to secure a better deal for himself with Fiat, angering and embarrassing “The Deuce” to the point that Ford wrote a blank check to beat Ferrari at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. While Ford achieved its goal in 1966, it seems the company still holds something of a grudge. Meet the Ford GT41, the new Hypercar that Ford is hoping will put it back on the top step at Le Mans.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 75062

The GT41 gets its name because, you guessed it, the air intake at the top of the car measures 41 inches above the ground. Well, technically, the GT41 stands at 41.7 inches tall, but Ford executives told Car and Driver that they preferred the sound of GT41 over GT41.7, and they had no interest in rounding up.

The GT41’s power is naturally aspirated, of course; this is an American race team, after all, though it is mated to a hybrid system as required by regulations. Still, the combustion part of the equation is handled by a Coyote V-8 engine that has been bored to 5.4 liters and developed in-house by Ford Racing engineers.

Despite a fair amount of grandstanding about how proudly American this program is—note the American flag, eagle, football, and Statue of Liberty graphics in the livery, along with timing the reveal to take place during the Detroit Lions game on the distinctly American holiday known as Thanksgiving—Ford still won’t commit to racing the GT41 in IMSA, here in North America. The final race livery will be revealed ahead of the 2027 WEC season’s opening race in Qatar, which will take place in March.

#4273. Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories

Unlike ordinary body fat, brown fat burns calories to generate heat, making it an attractive target for future obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of Basel and University Hospital Basel have now investigated whether medication can switch on this energy-burning tissue in humans. Their surprising findings suggest that harnessing brown fat with drugs may be more challenging than anticipated.

While white fat primarily serves as an energy reserve, brown adipose tissue uses energy to keep the body warm. People with more active brown fat also tend to be leaner and have better metabolic health.

Exposure to cold naturally activates brown fat, prompting scientists to search for medications that could mimic this response. A research team led by Professor Matthias Betz at the University of Basel and University Hospital Basel examined whether activating a specific receptor, known as the beta2 adrenergic receptor, could stimulate brown fat in humans. Their findings were published in the journal Cell Metabolism.

Drug Boosts Calorie Burning Without Clear Brown Fat Activation

To investigate, the researchers conducted two experiments involving 11 healthy volunteers. They compared the effects of mild cold exposure with those of fenoterol, a medication that stimulates beta2 adrenergic receptors. The scientists measured how much energy the participants expended and used PET/CT scans to monitor brown fat activity.

Both interventions caused the body to burn more energy. However, the scans revealed an important difference. Only cold exposure produced clear evidence of brown fat activation, with the tissue absorbing considerably more glucose than it did following fenoterol administration.

"We were surprised that energy expenditure increased strongly with fenoterol even though we could not detect a comparable activation of brown fat," says Betz. "Our study shows that an increase in energy expenditure does not automatically mean that brown fat has been activated."

Exactly where the additional energy is being consumed remains a mystery. The researchers suspect that fenoterol may increase energy consumption in other tissues, potentially including skeletal muscle or white fat.

Implications for Future Weight Loss Drugs

The findings also suggest that the biological mechanisms controlling brown fat in humans are more complex than previously thought. Analysis of human tissue indicates that fully activating brown fat may require the combined action of multiple receptors or biological signals rather than stimulating a single receptor.

Understanding these mechanisms could open new possibilities for treating obesity. Current weight loss medications work by reducing appetite. However, as people shed pounds, their bodies often compensate by burning fewer calories.

A treatment that simultaneously reduces appetite and increases calorie burning could help counteract this metabolic adaptation.

"Ideally, we could combine a reduction in appetite with an increase in energy expenditure," says Betz. "But first we need a better understanding of how brown adipose tissue is regulated."

Materials provided by University of Basel. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4270. World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

Robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Greater Precision Does Not Improve Recovery

Twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.

The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, said: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an important step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. We are very grateful for the support of the many patients who took part which is so important, but also the NIHR and Stryker for working so well together to support this critical study. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement."

Professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, said: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. These results are by no means a condemnation of the robotic systems, but more understanding of the ideal position for a knee replacement and personalization for each patient is needed. We'll then be able to truly take advantage of the advanced precision of robotic systems."

Professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, said: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. While this study shows robotic-assisted knee replacement is not yet improving patient outcomes, it highlights opportunities to refine these technologies and harness their precision to deliver better care in the future. The NIHR continues to fund robust studies, such as RACER, ensuring we learn how to deliver the latest technologies most effectively within the NHS."

Total knee replacement is among the most frequently performed elective surgical procedures worldwide for people with knee arthritis. During traditional surgery, orthopedic surgeons use standard surgical instruments and rely on their training and experience to position the artificial joint.

Robotic technology offers an alternative approach in which the surgeon controls a robotic arm during the operation. The system helps position surgical instruments with exceptional accuracy and allows surgeons to adjust the angles and depths of their cuts with greater flexibility. These capabilities make it possible to customize procedures to individual anatomy in ways that are not achievable with conventional techniques.

Landmark Trial Finds Similar Patient Outcomes

The study involved 339 patients treated by 33 surgeons at 10 hospitals across the UK. Despite the potential advantages of robotic technology, researchers found no meaningful difference between the two groups in the trial's primary outcome measure, the Forgotten Joint Score, one year after surgery.

This assessment measures how conscious patients are of their artificial joint while carrying out everyday activities. Ideally, a successful knee replacement allows patients to go about their daily lives without frequently noticing the artificial joint. Patients achieved similar scores regardless of which surgical technique was used.

Other measures also showed comparable results. These included walking ability, pain during hospitalization, pain during the first three months of recovery and at 12 months, and the likelihood of requiring another operation.

Researchers plan to monitor participants for ten years to determine whether differences between the two surgical approaches emerge over a longer period. One particularly important question is whether robotic assistance reduces the number of patients who eventually need additional knee surgery.

Robotic Knee Surgery Takes Longer and Costs More

Operations performed with robotic assistance required additional time (on average 10.5 minutes) and cost approximately £950 more per procedure.

Although the robotic system improved surgical precision, it was not associated with a higher risk of serious adverse events, indicating that the procedure appeared to be as safe as traditional knee replacement.

However, when assessed against current NHS spending thresholds, the robotic technology evaluated in the trial was not considered cost-effective during the first year following surgery.

The Future of Personalized Knee Replacement

The researchers believe that robotic technology could become more valuable if surgeons learn how to use its enhanced precision to better accommodate differences in individual patients' anatomy.

Determining the ideal placement of an artificial knee joint for each patient could eventually allow surgeons to turn greater technical accuracy into meaningful improvements in recovery, pain relief, and mobility. Achieving those benefits will require further technological development and additional research, making personalized robotic surgery a promising area for future investigation.

The findings of the RACER-Knee trial were published in The Lancet.

The research was organized by University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust and the University of Warwick. Funding was provided by the UK NHS research organization, the National Institute for Health Research, through its Health Technology Assessment Programme (NIHR128768).

Stryker, the company that manufactures the robotic system, covered the additional expenses associated with performing robotic surgery during the trial. The company did not participate in analyzing or interpreting the study results.

Materials provided by University of Warwick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4269. Where Does the Chevy Blazer SS EV Fit in Chevrolet’s SS History?

See our list of worthy and unworthy SS models to find out.

I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines. Chevy established the Super Sport trim in the 1960s with some legendary cars (Impala, Chevelle, Camaro, Nova) and then applied it scattershot over the decades, with some latter-day SS models worthy of the heritage and others an exercise in credibility dilution.

I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow). So here are my SS rankings, grouped by Worthy of the Name and Should Have Been an RS. Fun fact: One SS was both.

I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop? story. Our cop-evading candidates also included a Ferrari 488 GTB, and while the Ferrari was the quickest car of the day, the Camaro wasn’t as far behind as you might expect. It’s also possible that I just felt more comfortable pushing a Camaro than I did a Ferrari, but the SS 1LE remains the track-rat bargain of this century. I still want one.

See all results for new 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 90036

One of my high school hobbies was cadging test drives at car dealerships. Maybe I should have felt bad about wasting dealers’ time, but on some level I believed that I might actually buy whatever car I was begging for a drive. And I was arriving in my IROC, which was presentable enough to imply at least some trade-in value. I drove plenty of cars—the second-generation Ford Probe GT with its frisky V-6 was a pleasant surprise—but I did get shut down whenever I exceeded the threshold of deal-signing plausibility that was assigned when I rolled onto a given lot. That’s what happened when I asked to drive a 1994 Impala SS that was in the showroom of a local car dealer. I vividly remember what the salesman told me: “If everyone drives it, nobody buys it.” Instead, he gave me the keys to a Monte Carlo SS. I was amazed that a car with a similar engine to mine (the ubiquitous Chevy 5.0) could be so much slower. “Someday, I’ll write a story about how not all Chevys deserve an SS badge,” I probably didn’t say. But let’s imagine I did. What a perceptive lad!

I still haven’t driven a bubble-Caprice Impala SS. But I continue to revere them. They’re like a cop car, but cooler!

Speaking of cop-cars-but-cooler, the Chevy SS was the civilian version of the contemporary Caprice, and it was like Chevy’s version of an E39 BMW M5, complete with 415 horsepower and an available manual transmission. Of course, just right is never enough, so we had Lingenfelter Performance Engineering bolt on a supercharger before I took an SS on a multi-state investigation of the history of bootlegging. Sliding that car around on dirt roads out in moonshine country was so much fun I almost forgot I had a job to do. Which may or may not have involved bringing some things in the trunk back to Michigan. I get amnesia when I try to recall any details about that, but the SS—that I remember, and fondly. If you want one, maybe don’t wait too long, because the SS secret is out, based on what I see lurking on Bring a Trailer.

See all results for new 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 90036

I’ve never driven a Chevelle SS, but when we had one in a comparison test, it sounded like it was a royal handful. A 13.81-second quarter-mile at 102 mph isn’t super quick now, but consider that the first 500 feet of that run was probably devoted to wheelspin management as the 7.4-liter, 450-hp (gross-rated) V-8 abused the primitive tires of the day.

Of the Chevelle’s brakes, Sam Posey said, “While they’re working, they are predicta­ble.”

The Cobalt SS was a sneaky performance car when it debuted with a supercharged, 205-hp four-cylinder in 2005, and later got a 260-hp turbocharged upgrade. Chevy also built it in naturally aspirated form (hold that thought). This was around the time when GM started to figure out the concept of handling, and the Cobalt SS’s excellent all-around performance prompted me to conjure an unlikely contest in 2006. The premise: I race against Dale Earnhardt, Jr., around a tight road course at the Charlotte Motor Speedway infield. He’d get a Cobalt SS. And I’d get a 505-hp Corvette Z06. I beat him, but not for his lack of trying—he pushed that Cobalt so hard he pitted in with gravel falling out of the left-rear wheel because his track-out lines were starting to include real estate beyond the actual track.

Then we went Corvette to Corvette, and that went how you’d expect, as evidenced by his note in my Z06 press kit: “Good luck next time. Dale Jr., 30.8 (you 32.2).”

Dropping a dang Corvette engine in a family SUV is usually the sort of procedure that requires an engine hoist, a wrecked C4, and a long weekend. But in 2006 Chevy did that deed at the factory, giving us the Trailblazer SS, a 395-hp SUV that hit 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and conjured the casual menace of the ‘90s Impala SS. It also had upgraded brakes and suspension, modifications that our John Phillips described as “comprehensively testosteronated”. If you like the whole Trailblazer SS deal but wish it were weirder, GM also built a Saab version, the 9-7X Aero. It was about as Swedish as apple pie at a baseball game on the Fourth of July, and remains the most powerful Saab I can think of at the moment.

OK, the stopwatch doesn’t lie: the Blazer EV SS destroys its predecessors at the drag strip. The trip to 60 mph is over in 3.3 seconds, and the quarter-mile requires just 11.8 seconds. That beats an automatic 2019 Camaro SS (3.9 and 12.2 seconds for those respective runs), which itself was slightly quicker than the manual Camaro SSs we tested. On power alone—615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque—the electric Blazer deserves entry to the SS club.

In other ways, it’s merely casually sporty, but that’s been the SS mien in a lot of cases. I appreciate that you can get it in habanero orange, an extroverted hue that caused one of my kids to mistake it for a Lamborghini Urus for about 50 milliseconds. And, in this age of inflation, the $395 performance package is a huge bargain for the upgrades it brings: 22-inch summer tires and high-friction brake pads and rotors. Those front rotors are 15.3 inches and are grabbed by six-piston Brembo calipers. That’s legit hardware, as evidenced by its 157-foot stop from 60 mph.

The Blazer EV SS interior gives you some SS branding on the seats and steering wheel but otherwise looks mostly like any other Blazer EV, which is to say mostly like any other Chevy SUV. Which is fine. If I were the person at GM in charge of cost-benefit analysis, I too would opt for cruddy lower door plastic as long as I got to keep Super Cruise.

The Blazer EV SS is worthy of the SS badge. Whether it’s worthy of the Blazer one is a different discussion that you can continue on your forum, K5 Freaks 4EVR.

The positive news here was that Chevy brought back a V-8-powered Impala SS that was good at doing burnouts. The bad news was that it could barely avoid doing burnouts at all times because it was front-wheel-drive. Yes, Chevy dropped a dang 303-hp LS engine in the front-drive Impala of the day, resulting in torque steer that made every ditch a possibility. Our own Tony Quiroga described that Impala SS as a car that “gives the feeling that it’s waging war with itself”. Other observations from that review:

-“Keeping an 18-year-old platform competitive is not an insubstantial task.”

-“Dive, squat, and roll control could be described as nautical.”

-On the skidpad, “The Impala leaned over far enough to be included in Who's Who in Body Roll.”

-“Impressed by the 154-mph top speed? Driving the SS at that speed is scary enough to be a stunt on NBC's Fear Factor.”

-“The front-strut suspension crashes over pavement imperfections as if someone had overlooked the advantages of bushings.”

At the time, my wife had an Impala as a company car. She was a pharma sales rep for Johnson & Johnson, and her trunk was always full of Tylenol PM and K-Y Jelly. It would have been funny if she ever got pulled over and searched. Also, the second “A” of the trunk badge fell off, so we fondly referred to her car as the Impal. That was the right assignment for that era of Impala.

During the early-2000s hot-truck heyday, there were some wicked creations. Ford said, “Let’s put a 380-hp supercharged V-8 in a regular-cab two-wheel-drive F-150, call it the Lightning and do some huge burnouts.” Over at Dodge, they said, “Let’s drop a 500-hp Viper V-10 in a regular-cab, two-wheel-drive Ram, call it the SRT-10 and do some even huger burnouts.” When Chevy got in on the game, it said, “Let’s build a Silverado with an extended cab, all-wheel-drive, and 345 hp. We’ll call it the SS, and it won’t do burnouts.” Eventually Chevy built a rear-drive version, but the Silverado SS still got noogies and purple nurples at recess from the Dodge and Ford.

We said the Maxx itself was “a runty-looking cross between a family sedan and an ice chest,” and the SS treatment didn’t do a whole lot to energize that off-putting shape. The Maxx SS was powered by an iron-block pushrod V-6 that made all of 240 horsepower, sloshed to the front wheels by a four-speed automatic. It hit 60 mph in 6.9 seconds and topped out at a governed 115 mph. This Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be called an SS. In fact, this Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be at all. It reminded me of when I bought reflective mailbox lettering decals and made my parents’ rusty 1989 Subaru DL wagon the DL SS.

How is the Cobalt SS on both the worthy list and the SS trash pile? Because for two years, Chevy offered a naturally aspirated version that wheezed out just 170 horsepower. (The good version was formally named the Cobalt SS Supercharged.) Chevy itself got embarrassed by this SS’s half-heartedness and renamed it the Cobalt Sport after two years, proving that even pre-bankruptcy GM had limits to its cynicism. Happily, no subsequent SS stooped to that level, and hopefully none ever will.

Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

#4267. Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

Research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health. However, a new University of Michigan study warns that treating loneliness primarily as a health problem could shift responsibility away from society and place it on a healthcare system that lacks the tools to restore meaningful social connections.

Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.

Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences. One estimated that lacking social connections could be as harmful to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Another found that loneliness, social isolation, and living alone were each associated with an approximately 30% higher risk of premature death. The financial burden is also substantial, with separate research estimating that social isolation costs Medicare $6.7 billion each year in care for older adults.

"Once people saw these findings, they began to treat loneliness as urgent," said University of Michigan doctoral student Sofia Hiltner. "But it made me wonder: Why do we only consider problems important once they are tied to health?"

To understand how loneliness became a medical concern, Hiltner conducted interviews with experts and reviewed more than a decade of media coverage, medical journal articles, and academic literature.

Her analysis revealed that establishing a connection between loneliness and poor health helped the issue gain credibility. However, it also encouraged what she describes as a "logical leap": the belief that any problem affecting human health should become the responsibility of the healthcare system.

"Not everything that relates to health belongs in healthcare," she said. "Doctors can screen patients and connect them to services, but they cannot rebuild communities or shorten work hours."

Hiltner, a predoctoral trainee in social demography at the Population Studies Center within the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research, was inspired to investigate loneliness after witnessing her grandmother become increasingly isolated as she aged.

When Hiltner entered graduate school to research social isolation among older adults, she learned that clinical trials were investigating a "loneliness pill." The discovery prompted her to question why loneliness was being approached primarily as a medical condition rather than a social problem.

"After my grandfather died, my grandmother lived alone and there was little structure in her life," Hiltner said. "She didn't seem to have many friends or activities. It made me think about everything that happened throughout her life that led to that point. I wondered about the social policies, in addition to dynamics at the family level, that could have helped prevent that situation."

Finding Solutions Beyond the Healthcare System

Interestingly, Hiltner found that the medical community was initially reluctant to take responsibility for addressing loneliness. Much of the momentum behind incorporating loneliness into healthcare instead came from academic researchers, government health officials, and insurance companies.

Although recognizing loneliness as a medical concern can generate greater awareness and encourage intervention, it may also divert valuable resources from efforts to address the social circumstances that leave people isolated.

"There is the risk that defining loneliness as medical crowds out other ways of responding to the issue," she said. "Attention, time and resources are limited. On the other hand, framing it as medical may inspire more action than would have otherwise happened."

Hiltner hopes her findings will encourage policymakers to reconsider how they define social problems and explore preventive strategies that address their underlying causes before they develop into serious health concerns.

"I would like them to reflect on the strengths and limitations of addressing problems through the healthcare system, and look farther upstream to understand how a problem emerges, considering ways to intervene before it occurs," she said. "Healthcare can help, but it can only go so far."

#4263. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4262. One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia. However, new research from the University of Southern California (USC) suggests that the circumstances in which people are physically active may be just as important as the amount of activity they get.

An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, people who engaged in higher levels of physical activity at work appeared to face an increased risk of developing the condition.

Published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia. Already well established in cardiovascular research, this paradox refers to the observation that physical labor does not necessarily offer the same health advantages as recreational exercise and may even be associated with a greater risk of disease.

Led by David Raichlen, professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, the research team examined data from 74 cohort and case-control studies. Together, the studies included more than 4.2 million people between the ages of 45 and 93 from 30 countries. Over a median follow-up period of 10 years, researchers monitored diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia.

Participants who engaged in higher levels of recreational physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with the least active individuals. Physical activity associated with household chores also appeared to offer benefits, although this finding was supported by only one study. In contrast, higher levels of physical activity at work were linked to a 20% greater risk of dementia. Physically active commuting was also associated with a modest increase in risk, but evidence for this relationship came from just two studies.

"The findings challenge the long-held assumption that 'every move counts' for brain health," said Natan Feter, the study's first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen's Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil).

Why Exercise and Physical Labor May Affect the Brain Differently

Researchers often group recreational exercise, manual labor, household chores, and active commuting together when measuring "Physical activity." However, the authors suggest that the circumstances surrounding these activities vary considerably and could influence their long-term health effects.

People who exercise during their free time generally have greater control over the intensity and nature of their activities. Recreational exercise can also provide opportunities to socialize and relieve stress. In comparison, physically demanding occupations may require repeated movements, extended periods of standing, heavy lifting, and insufficient time to recover, along with exposure to potentially harmful workplace conditions.

The researchers do not believe that physical movement itself is likely to explain the elevated dementia risk associated with occupational activity. Instead, the relationship may arise from the social and environmental factors commonly associated with manual labor.

Physically demanding occupations are more likely to expose workers to psychological and social stress, limited control over their work, unsafe conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. Each of these factors has independently been associated with dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to participate in recreational exercise because of exhaustion, limited free time, or a lack of access to safe spaces for physical activity.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between physical activity and dementia risk was not linear and followed opposite patterns depending on the type of activity.

As recreational exercise increased, dementia risk gradually declined until the apparent benefits leveled off. Occupational physical activity showed the reverse pattern, with dementia risk increasing at higher activity levels before eventually reaching a plateau.

Important Limitations and Unanswered Questions

The authors emphasize that there is still too little research on physical activity related to household chores and commuting to draw definitive conclusions about either. Most of the available evidence also comes from high-income countries, despite projections that low- and middle-income nations will experience the greatest increases in dementia cases in the coming decades.

Another limitation is that almost all the studies depended on participants reporting their own physical activity. This approach can introduce errors if people do not accurately remember their activity levels. Nevertheless, Feter said the consistency of the findings across several additional statistical analyses suggests that the observed relationships warrant serious attention.

The researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from pursuing physically active occupations. Since the analysis relied on observational research, it cannot establish that occupational physical activity causes dementia.

Instead, the results underscore the importance of examining the conditions under which people are physically active. Recreational exercise continued to be associated with a lower risk of dementia, while occupational activity remained linked to a higher risk even after researchers accounted for differences in age, education, and chronic health conditions.

How Sedentary Activities May Also Influence Brain Health

The importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. Separate research by Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues, published recently in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, suggests that different types of sedentary behavior may also be associated with differences in brain structure.

In that study, mentally stimulating activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in certain regions of the cerebral cortex than more passive activities, such as watching television. These differences included brain regions involved in executive function.

Together, the findings could have important implications for public health strategies aimed at reducing dementia risk. The authors suggest that encouraging people to "move more" may not be sufficient without also addressing the circumstances in which physical activity takes place.

"In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself," Raichlen said. "Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself."

Raichlen and Feter's co-authors include Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M. Luong, Jack Gunnink, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan and Ashley Ventura of USC; Eduardo Caputo, Jayne Feter, Gustavo S. Silva and Airton José Rombaldi of Universidade Federal de Pelotas (Brazil); Paula Iso-Markku of the University of Helsinki (Finland); Daniela Benzano Bumaguin of Fundação Universitária de Cardiologia (Brazil); Yann C. Klimentidis and Gene E. Alexander of the University of Arizona; Daniel Umpierre and Natália Schröder of Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil); and Pedro C. Hallal of University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Funding for the research included National Institutes of Health grants P30AG072980, P30AG019610, R56AG067200, R01AG064587 and R01AG072445, along with support from the state of Arizona, the Arizona Department of Health Services and the McKnight Brain Research Foundation. Additional financial support was provided in part by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul (FAPERGS) (25/2551-0002834-5) and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development - CNPq and Department of Science and Technology of Secretariat of Science, Technology, Innovation and Health Complex of Ministry of Health of Brazil - MoH (445538/2023-6).

#4259. Gooseneck Hitches Explained

If a run-of-the-mill rear-mounted hitch won’t do, then a gooseneck hitch may be worth looking into.

Looking to tow a bigger and heavier trailer to carry the likes of livestock trailers, heavy equipment, or other vehicles? Then you’re probably going to need a heavy-duty pickup truck that’s both capable of pulling such a hefty load and compatible with towing a gooseneck-style trailer hitch.

This type of hitch gets its name from the high arch of steel that protrudes from the front end of the trailer. Goosenecks are designed to clear a pickup truck’s tailgate and sides, since the ball hitch the trailer connects to sits squarely in the middle of the tow-vehicle’s bed.

Placing the mount right over the truck’s rear axle enables more of the accompanying trailer’s weight to push down on the tow vehicle’s rear end. The result? The combined truck and trailer benefit from greater stability once on the move.

Fitting a gooseneck hitch to your truck is a completely different process relative to that of your typical rear-mounted hitch that hides under the bumper. You (or the manufacturer or service center) will need to drill right into the bed to install and mount the ball hitch and the accompanying safety chain attachment points.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

It’s a less invasive process than you may initially think, though. This is because the business end of a gooseneck is usually a long cylinder that sticks straight up from the bed.

In theory, this setup is similar to that of a fifth wheel hitch. In reality, a fifth wheel hitch is a different beast. Notably, fifth wheel setups require a much bulkier kingpin and jaw-style bed-mounted hitch. This setup provides quieter operation and additional stability at speed relative to a gooseneck hitch, and is often used for the towing of recreational trailers designed for the likes of camping.

The ball mount and coupler of a gooseneck, however, make this the heartier hitch for towing heavy tonnage. We’re talking north of 30,000 pounds in some instances.

Credit the fact that a gooseneck hitch pushes a large amount of the trailer’s mass downward onto the truck’s rear end, which allows the trailer to better resist sway than if it were mounted to a conventional tow hitch. The hitch’s in-bed location also allows the truck to handle heavier loads.

Another benefit of the in-bed ball hitch is that it takes up far less space than a fifth wheel. This means a majority of the bed remains available for its intended purpose: hauling cargo.

So, what can you haul with a hitch that’s ready for gooseneck trailering duty? Well, there are about as many options as there are jobs on a worksite. The most flexible choice is a flatbed trailer, which can carry anything from secured payloads to heavy construction equipment. Other options include livestock carriers, dumping trailers, and car haulers.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

Goosenecks also hold up well under abuse thanks to the tough but simple nature of the aforementioned ball hitch and coupler that connect the trailer and truck. It’s why gooseneck-style hitches are often used in agricultural and construction environments.

Installation aside, a gooseneck hitch is a simpler and safer way to tow big loads without having to sacrifice much in the way of in-bed utility. Not everyone needs a gooseneck hitch to tow with, but those who do are sure to benefit from the extra capability this style of hitch provides.

Both hitch types are sturdy options for towing heavy loads, but gooseneck hitches, the strongest of which can handle more than 30,000 pounds of weight, are generally regarded as the more capable heavy-duty hitch.

In theory, just about any pickup can be fitted with a gooseneck hitch. In practice, however, adding a gooseneck hitch to a light-duty pickup makes little sense given the lower payload and tow ratings of these trucks relative to their heavy-duty stablemates.

The in-bed connection point between the ball and the coupler of a gooseneck effectively makes towing with this type of hitch safer than towing with a run-of-the-mill bumper-pull hitch—particularly when towing especially heavy loads. Credit the fact that gooseneck hitches put more of the trailer’s weight directly over the tow vehicle’s rear axle. Because of this, gooseneck hitches typically offer far greater towing stability relative to that of a truck and trailer connected by a bumper-pull-type hitch.

#4257. A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar

Continuous glucose monitors help millions of people with diabetes keep track of their glucose levels in real time, making it easier to manage medications, dietary choices, and everyday activities. However, the high cost of these devices prevents some patients from accessing the technology.

Scientists at Texas A&M University have identified a potential way to make future glucose monitors more affordable. In a study published in ACS Measurement Science AU, the researchers found that a key sensing material for an experimental injectable glucose sensor performed just as well as a commonly used alternative at approximately one-tenth of the cost.

Many existing glucose monitoring technologies depend on enzymes to detect glucose. The Texas A&M team is pursuing a different approach that uses fluorescent molecules and near-infrared light. By measuring variations in the fluorescent signal, researchers can determine changes in glucose concentration without relying on enzymes.

The technology relies on a process called competitive binding. Within the sensor, glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete to occupy binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose levels rise, this competition alters the fluorescent signal, providing a way to measure glucose concentration.

After evaluating several compounds that bind to the protein, the team identified β-mannopentaose as a promising alternative to α-mannopentaose, a more expensive compound used in previous versions of the sensor. Despite its substantially lower price, β-mannopentaose delivered comparable sensing performance. It also produced promising results in artificial interstitial fluid, a laboratory solution that recreates conditions beneath the skin.

"The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative," said Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, assistant research scientist in Texas A&M's Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study's lead author. "In this case, the cheaper option wasn't really a compromise, and that's an important finding when you're thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies."

"Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together," said Dr. Gérard L. Coté, principal investigator of the study and a professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering. "This study shows that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development."

A Tiny Injectable Sensor Beneath the Skin

To create an injectable sensor, the researchers embedded the glucose detection materials within a small hydrogel designed to remain in the tissue beneath the skin. The gel holds the sensing materials in place while allowing glucose molecules to move through it, where their concentration can be measured.

During laboratory experiments, more than 94% of the sensing assay remained within the hydrogel after seven days. The results demonstrate that the less expensive sensing chemistry is compatible with an injectable glucose monitoring system.

"When new medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited," said Dr. Melissa Grunlan, study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. "Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them."

Although the experimental sensor has shown encouraging results, it remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Further development and testing will be necessary before the technology can be considered for clinical use. Nevertheless, the findings indicate that reducing material costs does not necessarily require sacrificing sensing performance.

Making Diabetes Monitoring More Accessible

The research highlights the importance of factoring affordability into the design of new medical technologies from the outset. Finding ways to reduce manufacturing expenses while maintaining performance could eventually expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly among patients who cannot currently afford advanced monitoring devices.

The researchers intend to further refine their technology and investigate other components that could enhance its performance, extend its useful lifespan, and make it more practical.

"While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results," Tripathy said.

"Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage," Coté said. "Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them."

The research team consisted entirely of Texas A&M researchers. Alongside Tripathy, Coté, and Grunlan, the team included Dr. Carolina Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, and Samyucktha Ganesapandian. Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Engineering Research Center for Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Under-resourced Populations.
